idiom_name: global/static let (computed lazily, once) / lazy var
implementation_notes: Swift computes global constants and variables lazily by definition - the language reference states that global constants and variables are always computed lazily, like lazy stored properties - and a stored type property (static let) is likewise initialized on first access, so no guard object or counter is needed and there is no observable uninitialized global. Use a static let on an enum or struct as the shared instance and the `lazy` modifier for a deferred instance property. The classic structure has no counterpart here; the decisions that remain are about thread safety and generics.
pitfalls: A lazy var is not documented as safe against concurrent first access from several threads: guard it or move the value behind a static let/actor when two threads can touch it.
A static stored property inside a generic type is initialized per specialization, so 'the' singleton exists once per concrete type argument; and duplicated frameworks can each keep their own copy.
Global initialization runs on whichever thread touches it first, so a heavy initializer adds latency to an arbitrary call rather than to launch, and nothing about it is ordered against main().
If the initializer traps (force unwrap, fatalError), the process dies at first use - which is harder to diagnose than dying at startup; keep globals inert and fallible work explicit.
